Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage.

2

Achieving equity requires action to empower health services, systems and communities to recognise and respond to social, cultural, commercial, and environmental determinants of health that impact access to care.

3

4

The Australian Cancer Plan highlights and aims to address disparities in cancer outcomes that exist between defined groups of the Australian population. Intersectionality can compound inequities and it is important to recognise that for many people, overlapping factors influence their cancer risk, diagnosis, treatment access and outcomes.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

People in lower socioeconomic groups

People living in rural and remote areas

intersex and asexual (LGBTQIA+) people

Older Australians

diverse backgrounds

Adolescents and young adults

Equity must be embedded in the delivery of care across the cancer continuum. To improve cancer experience and outcomes, equity must be embedded in the delivery of care across the cancer continuum. This includes providing tailored, appropriate, and adequately resourced services to all Australians in need – when, where, and how they need them.

To enable equitable delivery of optimal cancer care and meet the needs of priority populations, primary, secondary and tertiary health services and the community sector need to work together across geographic areas and public and private services.

Considerations for specific population groups:

18

Person-centred care means informing and involving people in their care, and respecting and responding to their individual needs, preferences and values, as well as those of their families and carers.

19

Person-centred care improves the experience for everyone involved, strengthens the quality and safety of care, and reduces the cost of care.

Person-centred care assumes an individual has capacity to make decisions for themselves. Where this is not the case, the multidisciplinary team should identify a substitute decision-maker who understands the person’s wishes and who is empowered to make decisions on behalf of the person under state / territory law.

Understand what matters and deliver care that responds to individual needs and preferences

Discuss and agree goals of care

Respect and respond to complex needs

Enable informed choice and informed consent

Use digital health appropriately

Enable shared care

Practise family-, carer and community-centred and inclusive care

<Additional information boxes linked from points above>

Understand what matters

Decisions about cancer care are not only influenced by cancer type, stage of disease and other health conditions.

Factors such as age, stage of life, culture, gender, and where a person lives and works, shape what is important for people with cancer and their families and carers.

Delivering care that responds to individual needs and preferences includes:

• challenging unconscious bias, racism and ageism

• asking people how they identify

20

21

• practising culturally safe, , trauma-informed care

• considering place-based approaches to care.

Discuss and agree goals of care

Goals of care for cancer include:

• treatment intent (e.g. curative vs symptom control)

• personal goals (e.g. being well enough to work, travel or participate in an important family event)

22

• consideration of how the person wants to engage in healthcare.

Goals of care can change over time and require review at key transition points.

23

24

Enable informed choice and consent ,

People have the right to understand what is involved in any test, procedure or intervention related to cancer care.

Health professionals must enable informed choice and are legally required to obtain informed consent from the person, or their substitute decision-maker, before any test, procedure or intervention.

Informed choice and informed consent apply to:

• options, benefits and risks of tests, procedures and interventions

• financial costs of tests, procedures and interventions

• what health and personal information will be collected and how it will be used

• genetic testing

• participation in research.

25

26

Use digital health appropriately ,

The growth of digital technology in cancer care brings challenges and opportunities for person-centred care.

Health professionals should consider the role that telehealth and other forms of digital health can play in enabling person-centred care. In doing so it is important to understand people’s access to and confidence in using digital technology as part of their care.

27

Enable shared care

Shared care supports person-centred care by providing care closer to home, reducing duplication, and involving health professionals involved in other aspects of a person’s healthcare.

Care can be shared between a cancer specialist and primary care provider, between different cancer specialists, or between cancer specialists and a nurse or allied health professional. Family members and carers can also play an active role in shared care.

28

29

Practise family-, carer-and community-centred / inclusive care ,

For many people, person-centred care means care that is inclusive of family and carers. For some people, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, this extends to community.

Family, carers and community provide important support for people across the cancer care continuum and have their own information and support needs.

Health professionals should proactively integrate family, carers and community into cancer care to the extent the person receiving cancer care wants them involved.

30

31

Key actions for delivering person-centred care ,

✓

Involve the person in decisions about their cancer care

✓

Involve family and carers to the extent the person would like them involved

✓

Find out what is important to the person, their families and carers and tailor communication and care accordingly, with consideration to:

•

life stage, experiences, culture and beliefs

•

literacy, health literacy, digital literacy and preferred language

✓

Provide timely and accessible information to enable informed choices about cancer care according to individual preferences and goals, including information about:

•

all options for tests or treatments and associated advantages and disadvantages

•

where care will be delivered and likely waiting times

•

timeframes in which decisions are needed

•

costs, including public and private options and out-of-pocket expenses

✓

Discuss and agree goals of care and revisit these at key transition points

✓

Discuss options and preferences for shared care

✓

32

Use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) to understand and respond to peoples’ needs and preferences

✓

33

Obtain informed consent for all tests, procedures and interventions from the person or their substitute decision-maker

Safe and quality care means delivering the most appropriate and best-value care, while keeping people safe from preventable harm in the delivery of that care.

Delivery of safe and quality cancer care is influenced by:

•

individual factors, such as patient age and stage of life

•

clinical factors, such as stage of disease and co-morbidities

•

service factors, such as the setting in which care is delivered

•

35

system factors, including national and state/territory policies and regulations and approved and reimbursed tests and treatments.

Safety and quality at all levels should include clinical considerations alongside issues of bias, cultural safety, racism and other factors that may compromise how a person accesses or experiences care.

sections.headingText: Considerations for safety and quality in cancer care
sections.headingPrinted: Considerations for safety and quality in cancer care
sections.content:
Deliver cancer care by appropriately trained and credentialled health professionals

Ensure appropriate capability and staffing of health services providing cancer care

Deliver evidence-based care

Deliver data-informed care

Enable and undertake research to drive quality improvement

Use digital health and technology appropriately

<Additional information boxes linked from points above>

Trained and credentialled health professionals

Cancer care should be provided by health professionals with training and experience appropriate to the cancer type and individual characteristics such as age, stage of life, co-morbidities, culture and language.

Individual OCPs contain details of specific training required for the delivery of care for specific cancer types and population groups.

Health service capability

Health services providing cancer care must have equipment, staff, policies and procedures required to support safe, high-quality care.

While person-centred care aims to provide care as close to home as safely possible, some aspects of diagnosis and treatment can only be undertaken safely in specialist centres and may require the person to travel.

Where evidence demonstrates improved outcomes in high-volume or specialist centres, referral to appropriately experienced multidisciplinary services should be considered.

Individual OCPs contain details of specific training required for the delivery of care for specific cancer types and population groups

Evidence-based care

Cancer care should be informed by best available evidence with reference to:

• national and international clinical practice guidelines

• evidence-based treatment protocols

• validated models of care.

Individual OCPs contain details of clinical practice guidelines, protocols and models of care relevant to cancer types and population groups.

Data-informed quality care

Services and health professionals delivering cancer care should collect, review and act on relevant data to inform evidence-based, high-quality care.

Measuring capabilities and performance against the OCPs can identify improvements to drive better and equitable patient outcomes.

Data sets relevant to cancer care include:

36

• National Cancer Control Indicators

37

• Kulay Kalingka Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cancer Control Indicators

38

• Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs)

39

• Patient-reported experience measures (PREMs)

40

• Radiation oncology clinical indicators.

Individual cancer-specific and population-based OCPs contain details of data sets relevant to cancer types and population groups.

Research

Research is an important driver of evidence-based care and can increase the quality and safety of care for people with cancer.

Individual OCPs contain details of research and clinical trial considerations at different pathway steps, relevant to cancer types and population groups.

Use of digital health and technology

Use of digital health and artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing across healthcare, leading to new considerations and associated standards for safety and quality. Examples include standards for:

AI and social media also present challenges in relation to misinformation for people at risk of and diagnosed with cancer.

✓

✓

✓ Embed clinical practice guidelines and protocols into local models of care to enable delivery of evidence-based care

✓ Routinely collect and contribute to relevant minimum cancer-related datasets to support benchmarking, quality care and service improvement, including population-specific data to enable benchmarking and quality improvement in relation to equity and inclusion.

Multidisciplinary care

50

Multidisciplinary care is an integrated team approach that involves all relevant health professionals discussing all relevant treatment options and making joint recommendations about treatment and supportive care plans that consider the individual characteristics and preferences of the person with cancer.

51

Multidisciplinary care improves outcomes for people with cancer, including survival.

52

The multidisciplinary team should include core disciplines that are integral to providing good care. Team membership should reflect both clinical and supportive care aspects of care. Pathology and radiology expertise are essential.

Core members of the multidisciplinary team are expected to attend most multidisciplinary meetings either in person or remotely via virtual mechanisms. The person’s GP is a core member of the team and should be actively engaged and informed from the point of diagnosis.

Australia has strong cancer outcomes overall, with survival rates for many cancers among the best in the world. However, cancer outcomes are not equal for all Australians. Disparities are influenced by many factors, including differences in access to cancer services, specialist expertise and multidisciplinary care across the country.

Australian Comprehensive Cancer Network (ACCN)

The aims to address these disparities through an integrated national network that connects cancer services across Australia.

The ACCN brings together services, networks and alliances, Comprehensive Cancer Centres, and other specialist providers to strengthen collaboration, facilitate the sharing of expertise, and support access to high-quality, coordinated cancer care for all Australians

Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care.

60

Supportive care is an essential component of cancer care that requires multidisciplinary input and interventions. It is needs based and is important for people with cancer, their families and carers. Supportive care is important across all steps of the optimal care pathway. Definitions and frameworks have evolved over time, incorporating elements of survivorship care and palliative care.

Supportive care for people with cancer, their families and carers can be considered in five key domains.

Physical: physical symptoms and side effects that may be acute, relatively short-lived or ongoing, requiring continuing interventions or rehabilitation

Psychological: issues related to the person’s emotional and mental health wellbeing

Social: social and practical issues that affect the person, their family and carers

Informational: information needs about cancer across the care pathway

Spiritual: relating to a person’s changing sense of self and challenges to their underlying beliefs and existential concerns

<Additional information boxes linked from points above>

Physical symptoms

Common physical symptoms associated with cancer include:

• anaemia

• ascites

• cardiotoxicity

• changes in appearance

• decline in mobility

• fatigue

• fertility changes

• fever

• insomnia

• nausea and vomiting

• neutropenia

• pain

• weight loss or gain

Psychological symptoms

Common psychological symptoms associated with cancer include:

• anger

• anxiety

• changes in cognition

• depression

• fear

• grief

• guilt

• shame

Social impacts

Common social impacts of cancer include:

• carer responsibilities

• impact on children

• impact on education

• finance

• intimacy / sexuality

• isolation

• legal impacts

• relationships

• travel

• working / return to work

Informational needs

People with cancer have informational needs across the care continuum and across all domains of supportive care.

Preferences for the amount and format of information vary and preferences may change at different times.

Carers and family members also require information and their needs and preferences may differ to those of the person with cancer.

Spiritual needs

Spiritual needs include but are not limited to:

• existential concerns and fears

• impact on faith

• impact on sense of self.

Key actions for implementing supportive care

✓ Embed supportive care screening into models of care across the care pathway with clearly defined responsibilities and strategies to act on the information collected

✓ Collect and use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and patient-reported experience measures (PREMs)

✓ Assess and screen people and their families and carers to understand supportive care needs across each of the five domains

– the additional burden of age, physical or cognitive disability, mental illness

– factors related to life stage, including carer responsibilities

– cultural considerations

– barriers to accessing supportive care services including geography, cost or disability

– carer, family and community needs

✓ Consider needs and tailor support that reflects individual as well as clinical considerations, including:

✓ Provide people with information to enable and empower them to articulate, understand, self-manage and seek support for their supportive care needs

✓ Refer people to appropriate services and organisations, including community and non-government organisations, who can provide timely support to optimise recovery

✓ Use evidence-based, multidisciplinary approaches to management of symptoms and side effects

✓ Provide information and skills training, as required, to people and their families and carers for home-based care

Navigation and care coordination

61

Navigation and care coordination are related person-centred interventions that aim to empower patients, families and carers affected by cancer to facilitate safe and timely access to optimal cancer-related care and support.

sections.headingText: Components of navigation and care coordination
sections.headingPrinted: Components of navigation and care coordination
sections.content:
62

Navigation and care coordination are essential across the care pathway and include a range of inter-related components. Needs should be assessed regularly and particularly at key transition points.

Needs assessment enabling escalation or de-escalation of support

Provision of education and information, including in-language assistance

Connection and referral to appropriate clinical and supportive care

Understanding and removing barriers to care

Support for travel, accommodation and other logistics

Financial information and assistance

Enabling self-empowerment

Advocacy

Navigation and care coordination should take account of the needs of the individual as well as clinical considerations for their cancer, including factors such as:

•

age

•

geography

•

ethnicity

•

sexuality

•

language

•

physical or cognitive disability

•

cultural factors.

Key actions for enabling navigation and care coordination

✓

Communicate proactively and in a timely way with patients, their families and carers, using translation or interpreter services as required

✓

Use and act on insights from patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) and supportive care screening tools

✓

Use and share treatment plans, survivorship care plans and advance care directives

✓

Involve the person’s primary care provider in care from the point of diagnosis and maintain regular and timely communication

✓

Participate in multidisciplinary meetings

✓

Hold multidisciplinary assessment clinics and / or coordinate patient appointments to streamline access and care

✓

Use telehealth and virtual care to connect people to care

✓

Enable shared access to medical records for all members of the multidisciplinary team

✓

Prioritise timely availability of test results to enable recommendations and decision-making

63

Everyone involved in cancer-related care has a role in navigation and care coordination, including health professionals and administrative staff in cancer services, primary care and community organisations. Navigation should be:

•

integrated: providing seamless, effective, and efficient care that is fit for purpose and person-centred

•

multi-channel: using multiple communication channels and provider platforms that empower people to access information and support across multiple touchpoints

•

multidisciplinary: involving health professionals, informal carers and relevant community support personnel.

Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP)

The ACNNP is free to access and designed to help people affected by cancer, including families, friends and carers to navigate the health system, to find the information and support they need, when they need it. The program has three connected components.

Cancer Navigation Services

Cancer Navigation Service

form

The Cancer Council delivers navigation supports to help people impacted by cancer find high quality information and support, depending on their needs. Individuals can self-navigate using the Cancer Connect digital navigation platform, or access help to navigate available supports through the 13 11 20 phoneline. Individuals can be connected with services delivered not only by Cancer Council but also the broader ACNNP and cancer care ecosystem. Referrals can be made to Cancer Council via this .

Cancer Hub

The Cancer Hub is a collaboration between Canteen, Red Kite and Camp Quality, to support children and young people ages 0–25, and families with children or young people, who are impacted by any cancer. Services

form

include navigation and emotional support, such as case coordination, counselling and peer support. Cancer Hub can be contacted on 1800 431 312 and referrals can be made via this .

Cancer Care Nursing Services

Cancer Care Nurse Service

The McGrath Foundation is delivering Commonwealth-funded cancer care nurses in health and hospital services across Australia. Patients receiving cancer care in a region where a McGrath Nurse is placed have access to a range of supportive care types including practical, informational and emotional support. Contact the McGrath Foundation Nursing Program Team on 02 8962 6100 to understand if there is a nurse available in a particular area.

Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses

The Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia (PCFA) is also delivering specialist prostate cancer nurses around Australia. These nurses provide care and support to prostate cancer patients and their families across the cancer continuum. Contact PCFA on 1800 220 099 to find out if there is a nurse in a particular area.

Specialist Support Services

non-government organisations

Twelve are funded to provide disease-specific information and support tailored to the unique needs of particular cancer types. Support is available via telephone and digital means for patients, families, carers, and friends. Health professionals may also access the services for disease-specific advice to support their patients. Services available from each organisation differs depending on specific needs of the individual communities.

Referrals

Referrals can be made to any of the above services by health professionals on behalf of patients, or directly by the individual requiring support. Health professionals and consumers can contact the relevant organisation(s) directly using the details and links above. Support can be accessed from more than one organisation at any given time, depending on the needs of the individual.

Where a health professional or consumer is unsure what support is available or where to find support, they should contact Cancer Council on 13 11 20.

Good communication is an essential part of cancer care and a responsibility of everyone involved in healthcare across the cancer continuum.64

Delivery of optimal cancer care requires high-quality, consistent and timely communication.

This Principle refers to communication between health professionals and people at risk of or diagnosed with cancer, their families and carers. Communication between health professionals is covered in sections on Shared care and Navigation and care coordination.

sections.content:
Communication with patients, families and carers must take account of the individual needs and preferences, with respect for age, culture, language, hearing or visual impairments and literacy.

65

Communication in cancer care covers a breadth of topics and requires skills, practice and judgement.

Pathway step

Examples of key communication skills

2. Presentation, initial investigations and referral

3. Diagnosis, staging and treatment planning

sections.headingText: Formats and considerations for communication in cancer care
sections.headingPrinted: Formats and considerations for communication in cancer care
sections.content:
66

A range of considerations influence approaches to communication in cancer care. It is important not to make assumptions about communication preferences.

In-person

Face-to-face consultation should be the first option when delivering critical diagnosis information, a change in therapy or prescribing intensive treatment.

67

If face-to-face is not an option, consider video consultation and encourage the patient to have a support person present

Telehealth

68

Video and telephone are effective forms of communication with people with cancer

69

When considering options for telehealth, it is important to consider individual preferences, access to and familiarity with digital communication, and any sensory or cognitive issues

Digital and AI-enabled communication tools (clinician focused)

Digital and AI-enabled tools are increasingly used to support communication and documentation in cancer care. Examples include consultation recording, ambient scribing, note-taking, transcription and summarisation tools. These technologies may reduce administrative burden and support communication between health professionals, patients, families and carers. Health professionals should be transparent about how these tools are being used, ensure appropriate consent and privacy protections, and verify the accuracy of information generated.

Health literacy

70

Health literacy – and broader literacy – are influenced by age, education and learning opportunities, disability and access needs, culture and language

Digital literacy (person-focused)

High digital literacy can improve communication and empower people to manage their care. However, use of digital technologies with people who have low digital literacy can widen disparities. It is important to consider patient and carer confidence in using digital technologies.

Language

A professionally trained health interpreter (not a family member or friend) should be made available when communicating with people with limited English proficiency. Navigation of the Australian healthcare system can pose problems for those with a non-Anglo culture, and treatment teams should pay particular attention to supporting these patients.

Key actions for enabling communication

✓

Ask people about how they like to communicate, including:

•

who they would like to be present during consultations

•

assistance needed due to visual or hearing impairment

•

interpreter support

•

considerations for literacy or other factors influencing information comprehension or retention

✓

Encourage and support the involvement of family members and carers in appointments

✓

Identify whether a person has a substitute decision-maker and involve them in relevant discussions

✓

Use plain language and avoid jargon and complex medical terms

✓

Use diagrams and validated tools and / or decision aids (see examples) <hyperlink to Find out more to be added>

✓

Provide written information and / or links to digital sources of information including videos

✓

Consider providing a question prompt list before appointments and offering a recording of the discussion to assist with recall (see examples) <hyperlink to Find out more to be added>

✓

Encourage people to ask questions and voice concerns

✓

Check for understanding by asking the people to relay what you have discussed in their own words

✓

Be truthful and transparent but sensitive to the psychological impact of information being conveyed

✓

Allow time appropriate to the level of complexity and sensitivity of the discussion and decisions

✓ Seek consent before sharing information between healthcare providers or with families or carers

✓

Make efforts to involve people in discussions about their care, to the extent they are able, even if decision-making has been transferred to a substitute decision-maker

✓

Be respectful if a person asks for a second opinion



Do not make assumptions about a person’s communication preferences



Do not expect patients, their families or carers to convey information between health professionals



Do not rely on family members to act as interpreter unless there is no alternative



Do not use stigmatising language or reinforcing stereotypes

sections.content:
Clinical trials are the foundation for generating evidence to improve cancer outcomes. They are used to test a range of interventions including:

•

diagnostic tests

•

drug interventions

•

supportive care interventions

•

symptom management

•

pain control

•

survivorship care

•

health service interventions.

Clinical trials can provide options for cancer patients when other therapies have failed or are yet to be approved. For some cancer types, clinical trials are standard of care and may be a first-line treatment option.

Other types of clinical research include:

•

observational studies

•

qualitative research

•

implementation studies

•

health services research.

Key considerations about clinical trials

• Clinical trials are not available for all cancer types, stages of cancer or population groups

• Compassionate access schemes can be an alternative to accessing drug if a clinical trial is not available

– The decision to join a suitable trial is always the patient’s to make

• Informed consent for research participation and for data and tissue collection and storage are essential

– travel and accommodation support are increasingly available to support participation for people who need to travel to participate in a trial

– decentralised trials and teletrials provide access to trials closer to home

• Access to trials is an important consideration:

Key actions regarding clinical trial participation

✓

Look for suitable clinical trials for people with cancer and remain vigilant for opportunities based on a person’s changing medical status and diagnostic profile

✓

Discuss the benefits of clinical trial participation with patients, their families and carers

✓

Actively support participation of people with cancer in suitable trials, even if this requires referral to another service or centre

✓

Continue to provide comprehensive care for people on clinical trials to ensure consistency in navigation and provision of supportive care

✓

Be ready to acknowledge disappointment and provide support if a suitable trial is not available

✓

Consider referral to supportive care services to help people to navigate the emotional impact of a suitable trial not being available, particularly if treatment options are limited



Do not make assumptions about who is and is not suitable for a clinical trial

Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage.

Achieving equity requires action to empower health services, systems and communities to recognise and respond to social, cultural, commercial, and environmental determinants of health that impact access to care.

The Australian Cancer Plan highlights and aims to address disparities in cancer outcomes that exist between defined groups of the Australian population. Intersectionality can compound inequities and it is important to recognise that for many people, overlapping factors influence their cancer risk, diagnosis, treatment access and outcomes.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
People living in rural and remote areas
People living with a mental illness

Equity must be embedded in the delivery of care across the cancer continuum. To improve cancer experience and outcomes, equity must be embedded in the delivery of care across the cancer continuum. This includes providing tailored, appropriate, and adequately resourced services to all Australians in need – when, where, and how they need them.

To enable equitable delivery of optimal cancer care and meet the needs of priority populations, primary, secondary and tertiary health services and the community sector need to work together across geographic areas and public and private services.
Key actions for equitable cancer care
Services should collect and review data to understand disparities in cancer outcomes and their drivers to inform planning and delivery of equitable cancer care.

People working at all levels of a health service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on unconscious bias and institutional racism , to ensure that people do not experience disparities in access or care due to:
People working at all levels of the service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on cultural competence knowledge, awareness, behaviour, skills and attitudes. ,
People receiving cancer care should be asked how they identify to enable delivery of personalised and culturally safe care. How people identify must not influence the quality of care provided.

Services should be delivered with due consideration of the financial impact of cancer, its diagnosis and treatment, with information and support provided to reduce the risk and impact of financial toxicity.
Services delivering cancer care should utilise telehealth and flexible service models to enable access to services and support appropriate to the person’s location and circumstances.
Services should enable inclusive participation in appropriate clinical trials and research.
Services should apply co-design principles to ensure that services meet the needs and priorities of communities they are designed for.
Services delivering cancer care should have structures, services and environments appropriate to the age of people receiving care. , ,

All cancer care professionals should recognise the prevalence of trauma and be sensitive to and respectful of how past or ongoing trauma may impact a person’s engagement with health services and cancer care. This extends to the person’s family, carers and community.

Person-centred care means informing and involving people in their care, and respecting and responding to their individual needs, preferences and values, as well as those of their families and carers.
Person-centred care improves the experience for everyone involved, strengthens the quality and safety of care, and reduces the cost of care.

Person-centred care assumes an individual has capacity to make decisions for themselves. Where this is not the case, the multidisciplinary team should identify a substitute decision-maker who understands the person’s wishes and who is empowered to make decisions on behalf of the person under state / territory law.
Understand what matters and deliver care that responds to individual needs and preferences
Discuss and agree goals of care
Respect and respond to complex needs
Enable informed choice and informed consent

Decisions about cancer care are not only influenced by cancer type, stage of disease and other health conditions.
Factors such as age, stage of life, culture, gender, and where a person lives and works, shape what is important for people with cancer and their families and carers.
Delivering care that responds to individual needs and preferences includes:
• challenging unconscious bias, racism and ageism
Discuss and agree goals of care
Goals of care for cancer include:
• treatment intent (e.g. curative vs symptom control)
• personal goals (e.g. being well enough to work, travel or participate in an important family event)
• consideration of how the person wants to engage in healthcare.
Goals of care can change over time and require review at key transition points.
People have the right to understand what is involved in any test, procedure or intervention related to cancer care.
Health professionals must enable informed choice and are legally required to obtain informed consent from the person, or their substitute decision-maker, before any test, procedure or intervention.
Informed choice and informed consent apply to:
• options, benefits and risks of tests, procedures and interventions
• financial costs of tests, procedures and interventions
• what health and personal information will be collected and how it will be used
The growth of digital technology in cancer care brings challenges and opportunities for person-centred care.

Health professionals should consider the role that telehealth and other forms of digital health can play in enabling person-centred care. In doing so it is important to understand people’s access to and confidence in using digital technology as part of their care.
Shared care supports person-centred care by providing care closer to home, reducing duplication, and involving health professionals involved in other aspects of a person’s healthcare.

Care can be shared between a cancer specialist and primary care provider, between different cancer specialists, or between cancer specialists and a nurse or allied health professional. Family members and carers can also play an active role in shared care.
Practise family-, carer-and community-centred / inclusive care ,
For many people, person-centred care means care that is inclusive of family and carers. For some people, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, this extends to community.
Family, carers and community provide important support for people across the cancer care continuum and have their own information and support needs.
Health professionals should proactively integrate family, carers and community into cancer care to the extent the person receiving cancer care wants them involved.

Provide timely and accessible information to enable informed choices about cancer care according to individual preferences and goals, including information about:

Safe and quality care means delivering the most appropriate and best-value care, while keeping people safe from preventable harm in the delivery of that care.
Delivery of safe and quality cancer care is influenced by:
individual factors, such as patient age and stage of life
clinical factors, such as stage of disease and co-morbidities
service factors, such as the setting in which care is delivered
system factors, including national and state/territory policies and regulations and approved and reimbursed tests and treatments.

Safety and quality at all levels should include clinical considerations alongside issues of bias, cultural safety, racism and other factors that may compromise how a person accesses or experiences care.

Multidisciplinary care is an integrated team approach that involves all relevant health professionals discussing all relevant treatment options and making joint recommendations about treatment and supportive care plans that consider the individual characteristics and preferences of the person with cancer.
Multidisciplinary care improves outcomes for people with cancer, including survival.

The multidisciplinary team should include core disciplines that are integral to providing good care. Team membership should reflect both clinical and supportive care aspects of care. Pathology and radiology expertise are essential.

Core members of the multidisciplinary team are expected to attend most multidisciplinary meetings either in person or remotely via virtual mechanisms. The person’s GP is a core member of the team and should be actively engaged and informed from the point of diagnosis.

Australia has strong cancer outcomes overall, with survival rates for many cancers among the best in the world. However, cancer outcomes are not equal for all Australians. Disparities are influenced by many factors, including differences in access to cancer services, specialist expertise and multidisciplinary care across the country.
The aims to address these disparities through an integrated national network that connects cancer services across Australia.

The ACCN brings together services, networks and alliances, Comprehensive Cancer Centres, and other specialist providers to strengthen collaboration, facilitate the sharing of expertise, and support access to high-quality, coordinated cancer care for all Australians

Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care.

Supportive care is an essential component of cancer care that requires multidisciplinary input and interventions. It is needs based and is important for people with cancer, their families and carers. Supportive care is important across all steps of the optimal care pathway. Definitions and frameworks have evolved over time, incorporating elements of survivorship care and palliative care.
Supportive care for people with cancer, their families and carers can be considered in five key domains.
Physical: physical symptoms and side effects that may be acute, relatively short-lived or ongoing, requiring continuing interventions or rehabilitation
Psychological: issues related to the person’s emotional and mental health wellbeing
Social: social and practical issues that affect the person, their family and carers
Informational: information needs about cancer across the care pathway
Spiritual: relating to a person’s changing sense of self and challenges to their underlying beliefs and existential concerns

Navigation and care coordination are related person-centred interventions that aim to empower patients, families and carers affected by cancer to facilitate safe and timely access to optimal cancer-related care and support.
Navigation and care coordination are essential across the care pathway and include a range of inter-related components. Needs should be assessed regularly and particularly at key transition points.
Needs assessment enabling escalation or de-escalation of support
Provision of education and information, including in-language assistance
Connection and referral to appropriate clinical and supportive care
Understanding and removing barriers to care
Support for travel, accommodation and other logistics
Navigation and care coordination should take account of the needs of the individual as well as clinical considerations for their cancer, including factors such as:
Key actions for enabling navigation and care coordination
Communicate proactively and in a timely way with patients, their families and carers, using translation or interpreter services as required
Use and act on insights from patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) and supportive care screening tools
Use and share treatment plans, survivorship care plans and advance care directives
Involve the person’s primary care provider in care from the point of diagnosis and maintain regular and timely communication
Hold multidisciplinary assessment clinics and / or coordinate patient appointments to streamline access and care
Use telehealth and virtual care to connect people to care
Enable shared access to medical records for all members of the multidisciplinary team
Prioritise timely availability of test results to enable recommendations and decision-making

integrated: providing seamless, effective, and efficient care that is fit for purpose and person-centred
multi-channel: using multiple communication channels and provider platforms that empower people to access information and support across multiple touchpoints
multidisciplinary: involving health professionals, informal carers and relevant community support personnel.

Australian Cancer Nursing and Navigation Program (ACNNP)

The ACNNP is free to access and designed to help people affected by cancer, including families, friends and carers to navigate the health system, to find the information and support they need, when they need it. The program has three connected components.

The Cancer Council delivers navigation supports to help people impacted by cancer find high quality information and support, depending on their needs. Individuals can self-navigate using the Cancer Connect digital navigation platform, or access help to navigate available supports through the 13 11 20 phoneline. Individuals can be connected with services delivered not only by Cancer Council but also the broader ACNNP and cancer care ecosystem. Referrals can be made to Cancer Council via this .

The Cancer Hub is a collaboration between Canteen, Red Kite and Camp Quality, to support children and young people ages 0–25, and families with children or young people, who are impacted by any cancer. Services
include navigation and emotional support, such as case coordination, counselling and peer support. Cancer Hub can be contacted on 1800 431 312 and referrals can be made via this .

The McGrath Foundation is delivering Commonwealth-funded cancer care nurses in health and hospital services across Australia. Patients receiving cancer care in a region where a McGrath Nurse is placed have access to a range of supportive care types including practical, informational and emotional support. Contact the McGrath Foundation Nursing Program Team on 02 8962 6100 to understand if there is a nurse available in a particular area.

The Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia (PCFA) is also delivering specialist prostate cancer nurses around Australia. These nurses provide care and support to prostate cancer patients and their families across the cancer continuum. Contact PCFA on 1800 220 099 to find out if there is a nurse in a particular area.

Twelve are funded to provide disease-specific information and support tailored to the unique needs of particular cancer types. Support is available via telephone and digital means for patients, families, carers, and friends. Health professionals may also access the services for disease-specific advice to support their patients. Services available from each organisation differs depending on specific needs of the individual communities.

Referrals can be made to any of the above services by health professionals on behalf of patients, or directly by the individual requiring support. Health professionals and consumers can contact the relevant organisation(s) directly using the details and links above. Support can be accessed from more than one organisation at any given time, depending on the needs of the individual.

Communication with patients, families and carers must take account of the individual needs and preferences, with respect for age, culture, language, hearing or visual impairments and literacy.

Digital and AI-enabled communication tools (clinician focused)

Digital and AI-enabled tools are increasingly used to support communication and documentation in cancer care. Examples include consultation recording, ambient scribing, note-taking, transcription and summarisation tools. These technologies may reduce administrative burden and support communication between health professionals, patients, families and carers. Health professionals should be transparent about how these tools are being used, ensure appropriate consent and privacy protections, and verify the accuracy of information generated.
Health literacy – and broader literacy – are influenced by age, education and learning opportunities, disability and access needs, culture and language

High digital literacy can improve communication and empower people to manage their care. However, use of digital technologies with people who have low digital literacy can widen disparities. It is important to consider patient and carer confidence in using digital technologies.

A professionally trained health interpreter (not a family member or friend) should be made available when communicating with people with limited English proficiency. Other types of clinical research include:
• Clinical trials are not available for all cancer types, stages of cancer or population groups
• Compassionate access schemes can be an alternative to accessing drug if a clinical trial is not available
– The decision to join a suitable trial is always the patient’s to make
• Informed consent for research participation and for data and tissue collection and storage are essential
– travel and accommodation support are increasingly available to support participation for people who need to travel to participate in a trial
– decentralised trials and teletrials provide access to trials closer to home
• Access to trials is an important consideration:
Key actions regarding clinical trial participation
Look for suitable clinical trials for people with cancer and remain vigilant for opportunities based on a person’s changing medical status and diagnostic profile
Discuss the benefits of clinical trial participation with patients, their families and carers
Actively support participation of people with cancer in suitable trials, even if this requires referral to another service or centre
Continue to provide comprehensive care for people on clinical trials to ensure consistency in navigation and provision of supportive care
Be ready to acknowledge disappointment and provide support if a suitable trial is not available

Do not make assumptions about who is and is not suitable for a clinical trial

checklistItems.text: Services should collect and review data to understand disparities in cancer outcomes and their drivers to inform planning and delivery of equitable cancer care. 5

People working at all levels of a health service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on unconscious bias and institutional racism 6 , 7 to ensure that people do not experience disparities in access or care due to: – age – gender – geography – ethnicity – sexuality – language – physical or cognitive disability – cultural or religious factors.
People working at all levels of the service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on cultural competence knowledge, awareness, behaviour, skills and attitudes. 8 , 9
People receiving cancer care should be asked how they identify to enable delivery of personalised and culturally safe care. 10 How people identify must not influence the quality of care provided.

Services should be delivered with due consideration of the financial impact of cancer, its diagnosis and treatment, with information and support provided to reduce the risk and impact of financial toxicity. 11
Services delivering cancer care should utilise telehealth 12 and flexible service models to enable access to services and support appropriate to the person’s location and circumstances.
Services should enable inclusive participation in appropriate clinical trials and research.
Services should apply co-design principles to ensure that services meet the needs and priorities of communities they are designed for. 13
Services delivering cancer care should have structures, services and environments appropriate to the age of people receiving care. 14 , 15 , 16

All cancer care professionals should recognise the prevalence of trauma and be sensitive to and respectful of how past or ongoing trauma may impact a person’s engagement with health services and cancer care. This extends to the person’s family, carers and community. 17

keyTableRows.rowLabel: Cancer Navigation Services
keyTableRows.content: Cancer Navigation Service The Cancer Council delivers navigation supports to help people impacted by cancer find high quality information and support, depending on their needs. Individuals can self-navigate using the Cancer Connect digital navigation platform, or access help to navigate available supports through the 13 11 20 phoneline. Individuals can be connected with services delivered not only by Cancer Council but also the broader ACNNP and cancer care ecosystem. Referrals can be made to Cancer Council via this . form Cancer Hub The Cancer Hub is a collaboration between Canteen, Red Kite and Camp Quality, to support children and young people ages 0–25, and families with children or young people, who are impacted by any cancer. Services
include navigation and emotional support, such as case coordination, counselling and peer support. Cancer Hub can be contacted on 1800 431 312 and referrals can be made via this . form

keyTableRows.rowLabel: Cancer Care Nursing Services
keyTableRows.content: Cancer Care Nurse Service The McGrath Foundation is delivering Commonwealth-funded cancer care nurses in health and hospital services across Australia. Patients receiving cancer care in a region where a McGrath Nurse is placed have access to a range of supportive care types including practical, informational and emotional support. Contact the McGrath Foundation Nursing Program Team on 02 8962 6100 to understand if there is a nurse available in a particular area. Prostate Cancer Specialist Nurses The Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia (PCFA) is also delivering specialist prostate cancer nurses around Australia. These nurses provide care and support to prostate cancer patients and their families across the cancer continuum. Contact PCFA on 1800 220 099 to find out if there is a nurse in a particular area.

keyTableRows.rowLabel: Specialist Support Services
keyTableRows.content: Twelve are funded to provide disease- specific information and support tailored to the unique needs of particular cancer types. Support is available via telephone and digital means for patients, families, carers, and friends. Health professionals may also access the services for disease-specific advice to support their patients. Support can be accessed from more than one organisation at any given time, depending on the needs of the individual. In-person | Face-to-face consultation should be the first option when delivering critical diagnosis information, a change in therapy or prescribing intensive treatment. If face-to-face is not an option, consider video consultation and encourage the patient to have a support person present 67 67 Cancer Australia 2022 A conceptual framework for cancer care during a pandemic incorporating evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic: Review and update July 2022 – Incorporating evidence review to June 2021

Telehealth | Video and telephone are effective forms of communication with people with cancer 68 68 Banbury A et al. APJCO 2023;19(6):752-761 Consumers’ experiences, preferences, and perceptions of effectiveness in using telehealth for cancer care in Australia When considering options for telehealth, it is important to consider individual preferences, access to and familiarity with digital communication, and any sensory or cognitive issues 69 69 Dykgraaf SH et al. AJGP 2022 Sep;51(9):721-724. Older people, the digital divide and use of telehealth during the COVID-19 pandemic

Digital and AI-enabled communication tools (clinician focused) | Digital and AI-enabled tools are increasingly used to support communication and documentation in cancer care. Examples include consultation recording, ambient scribing, note-taking, transcription and summarisation tools. These technologies may reduce administrative burden and support communication between health professionals, patients, families and carers. Health professionals should be transparent about how these tools are being used, ensure appropriate consent and privacy protections, and verify the accuracy of information generated.

Health literacy | Health literacy – and broader literacy – are influenced by age, education and learning opportunities, disability and access needs, culture and language 70 70 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Healthcare. Accessed 20 May 2026. Understanding health information (health literacy).

Digital literacy (person-focused) | High digital literacy can improve communication and empower people to manage their care. However, use of digital technologies with people who have low digital literacy can widen disparities. It is important to consider patient and carer confidence in using digital technologies.

Language | A professionally trained health interpreter (not a family member or friend) should be made available when communicating with people with limited English proficiency. Navigation of the Australian healthcare system can pose problems for those with a non-Anglo culture, and treatment teams should pay particular attention to supporting these patients.
